query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The retention of toughness in metastable face‐centered cubic high-entropy alloys is governed by the formation and migration of nano-twins at grain boundaries during deformation, which absorb strain energy and delay crack propagation.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic or near-equiatomic AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy processed to yield a metastable FCC structure with a propensity for nano-twin formation.
generation.intervention: A controlled compositional change by increasing the Al content to raise the stacking fault energy, which is expected to suppress nano-twin nucleation.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under both room temperature and cryogenic conditions using uniaxial tensile or compression loading, with constant grain size and processing history to isolate the twin effect.
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-twin density and their dynamic evolution at the grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Lower stacking fault energy in the baseline alloy promotes dynamic nano-twinning during deformation, which absorbs local strain energy and impedes crack propagation. By increasing the Al content, the stacking fault energy is raised, reducing nano-twin formation; this diminished twin contribution leads to lower toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the high-Al content alloy should exhibit a lower density of nano-twins during deformation and, consequently, reduced ductility and fracture toughness, despite similar yield strength.
generation.baseline: The standard equiatomic AlCoCrFeNi alloy with optimized nano-twin formation that yields high toughness.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate in FCC-phase high-entropy alloys with similar microstructural parameters (grain size, processing history) and within a compositional range that does not induce a phase change (e.g., maintaining single-phase FCC structure).
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative contribution of nano-twinning to toughness and the critical range of Al content that affects stacking fault energy without triggering other phase transformations remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two series of high-entropy alloy specimens: one with the baseline equiatomic AlCoCrFeNi composition and another with a systematically increased Al content. Ensure identical processing to produce metastable FCC structures. Subject the specimens to identical uniaxial tensile (or compression) tests at room and cryogenic temperatures while monitoring deformation.
measurements: Nano-twin density and distribution (using transmission electron microscopy)
Stacking fault energy estimation (via indirect measurement or simulation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the specimens with increased Al content do not show a statistically significant reduction in nano-twin density and exhibit comparable or improved fracture toughness relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis that toughness retention is controlled by nano-twinning is falsified.

Exceptional damage-tolerance of a medium-entropy alloy CrCoNi at cryogenic temperatures

Abstract: High-entropy alloys are an intriguing new class of metallic materials that derive their properties from being multi-element systems that can crystallize as a single phase, despite containing high concentrations of five or more elements with different crystal structures. Here we examine an equiatomic medium-entropy alloy containing only three elements, CrCoNi, as a single-phase face-centred cubic solid solution, which displays strength-toughness properties that exceed those of all high-entropy alloys and most multi-phase alloys. At room temperature, the alloy shows tensile strengths of almost 1 GPa, failure strains of ∼70% and KJIc fracture-toughness values above 200 MPa m1/2; at cryogenic temperatures strength, ductility and toughness of the CrCoNi alloy improve to strength levels above 1.3 GPa, failure strains up to 90% and KJIc values of 275 MPa m1/2. Such properties appear to result from continuous steady strain hardening, which acts to suppress plastic instability, resulting from pronounced dislocation activity and deformation-induced nano-twinning. Microstructure and composition dependence of mechanical characteristics of nanoimprinted AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys

Abstract: Molecular dynamics is applied to explore the deformation mechanism and crystal structure development of the AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys under nanoimprinting. The influences of crystal structure, alloy composition, grain size, and twin boundary distance on the mechanical properties are carefully analyzed. The imprinting load indicates that the highest loading force is in ascending order with polycrystalline, nano-twinned (NT) polycrystalline, and monocrystalline. The change in alloy composition suggests that the imprinting force increases as the Al content in the alloy increases. The reverse Hall–Petch relation found for the polycrystalline structure, while the Hall–Petch and reverse Hall–Petch relations are discovered in the NT-polycrystalline, which is due to the interactions between the dislocations and grain/twin boundaries (GBs/TBs). The deformation behavior shows that shear strain and local stress are concentrated not only around the punch but also on GBs and adjacent to GBs.
